```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_dplyr <- requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)
```

fewclust fits regression models for a binary outcome measured repeatedly
within a small number of groups: patients followed over a few visits,
clinics observed over a few months, classes over a few terms.  With few
groups the usual analyses (GEE with the standard sandwich, mixed models with
Wald tests on a normal reference) give tests that reject too often.
fewclust fits the methods that stayed calibrated in a simulation study of
these designs (see `vignette("simulation-study")`).

## A first fit

`fc_trial` is a small synthetic trial: a binary outcome `y` measured at 4
occasions (`time`) in each of 24 groups (`id`), with a group-level
treatment `arm` and a covariate `x`.

```{r}
library(fewclust)
fit <- fit_fewclust(fc_trial, y ~ time * arm, id = id, time = time)
fit
```

The data come first and the columns are given by name, so the function
works in a pipe and with tibbles:

```{r}
fc_trial |>
  fit_fewclust(y ~ time * arm + x, id = id, time = time) |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE)
```

The coefficients are marginal (population-averaged) log odds ratios: they
compare the probability of the event between groups of the population, as
with GEE, not within a group as with a mixed model.

## What the default does

`method = "auto"` (the default) fits the **marginalized multilevel model**
of Heagerty (1999).  With `time` the model has a first-order transition
term between consecutive observations of a group and a latent standard
deviation that may change linearly over the occasions.  A convergence check
replaces a trend fit at the boundary (or that did not converge) with the
fit with a constant latent standard deviation, if that fit converges with
finite estimates and standard errors; if it does not, the marginalized
model gives no result for the dataset.  The tests use a t
distribution with N - p degrees of freedom: N groups minus p coefficients.

If the marginalized model gives no usable estimate, `fit_fewclust()` fits
**GEE** with an AR(1) working correlation and the Fay-Graubard small-sample
correction, with the same t reference, and says so with a message.  A
coefficient is usable when its estimate and standard error are finite and
smaller than 10 on the logit scale.

`summary()` shows the details, including the convergence check:

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

## Choosing the method

```{r}
gee <- fit_fewclust(fc_trial, y ~ time * arm,
  id = id, time = time,
  method = "gee"
)
tidy(gee)
```

`corstr` sets the working correlation of GEE (`"ar1"`, `"exchangeable"`,
`"independence"`; by default `"ar1"` with `time` and `"exchangeable"`
without `time`, falling back to `"independence"` if the working correlation
degenerates) and `correction` the small-sample correction (`"fg"`, `"md"`,
`"kc"`, `"none"`).  Choosing anything other than the Fay-Graubard
correction gives a warning, because with few groups it was the most
reliable.  Because the marginalized model's standard errors are
model-based on both paths (with and without `time`), comparing against
`method = "gee"` is good practice when the model includes within-cluster
covariates whose effect may vary across groups (random slopes);
conversely, in GEE with time-varying covariates that may depend on prior
outcomes, `corstr = "independence"` avoids the full-covariate conditional
mean bias of Pepe and Anderson (1994).

## Errors, warnings, messages and notes

fewclust stops only when no estimate can be computed, and the error says
what to do:

```{r, error = TRUE}
d <- fc_trial
d$y <- 0
fit_fewclust(d, y ~ time * arm, id = id, time = time)
```

Warnings flag results that are less reliable than usual:

```{r}
few <- simulate_clustered_binary(n_groups = 8, n_occasions = 4, seed = 5)
fit8 <- fit_fewclust(few, y ~ time + arm, id = id, time = time)
```

Notes, printed with the fit, describe small designs.  With 2 or 3
occasions and at most 25 groups the models have little power and some
datasets give no usable estimate:

```{r}
short <- simulate_clustered_binary(n_groups = 12, n_occasions = 3, seed = 4)
fit_fewclust(short, y ~ time * arm, id = id, time = time)
```

Every condition has a class, `"fewclust_error"`, `"fewclust_warning"` or
`"fewclust_message"`, so you can catch or silence them selectively, for
example with `tryCatch(..., fewclust_error = function(e) NULL)`.

## A p-value for the smallest designs

`flip_test()` tests one coefficient with the sign-flip score test of
Hemerik, Goeman and Finos (2020).  It gives a p-value only, no estimate and
no interval, but it keeps its level with few groups and short series:

```{r}
flip_test(short, y ~ time * arm, id = id, time = time, seed = 1)
```

## Many fits

Fits are ordinary objects, so they combine with the tidyverse:

```{r, eval = has_dplyr}
sites <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  A = simulate_clustered_binary(n_groups = 20, seed = 1),
  B = simulate_clustered_binary(n_groups = 20, seed = 2),
  .id = "site"
)
sites |>
  dplyr::group_by(site) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(\(d, key) {
    tidy(fit_fewclust(d, y ~ time + arm, id = id, time = time))
  })
```

Inside your own functions, pass the column names with `{{ }}`:

```{r}
fit_by <- function(data, cluster) {
  fit_fewclust(data, y ~ time + arm, id = {{ cluster }}, time = time)
}
coef(fit_by(fc_trial, id))
```

## References

Heagerty PJ (1999). Marginally specified logistic-normal models for
longitudinal binary data. *Biometrics* 55(3), 688-698.

Fay MP, Graubard BI (2001). Small-sample adjustments for Wald-type tests
using sandwich estimators. *Biometrics* 57(4), 1198-1206.

Hemerik J, Goeman JJ, Finos L (2020). Robust testing in generalized linear
models by sign flipping score contributions. *Journal of the Royal
Statistical Society: Series B* 82(3), 841-864.

Konis K (2007). Linear programming algorithms for detecting separated data
in binary logistic regression models. DPhil thesis, University of Oxford.

Pepe MS, Anderson GL (1994). A cautionary note on inference for marginal
regression models with longitudinal data and general correlated response
data. *Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation* 23(4),
939-951.
